analysis.title: Attractive carry yields in bonds: Lock-in elevated yield levels with select medium tenor bonds
key_insights: UBS CIO sees bonds as attractive and prefers short-to-medium tenors in corporate bonds and up to 10-year maturities in high-quality bonds. High carry yields make positive total returns over 12 months very likely, in its view.

Re-accelerating energy end-product prices, possible El Niño-related food price inflation and stronger-than-expected US and European growth are delaying a decline in inflation and pushing central banks to be more restrictive. Market pricing of hikes has receded from excessive levels.

Following the October widening, corporate spread valuations have improved while overall yields remain near historic highs. UBS expects mid to high single-digit returns over the medium term, with fundamentals largely sound.
Selectivity is key in corporate credit. Uncertainty around growth, inflation, geopolitics and trade policy, plus M&A, bond supply and issuer-specific risks, should keep single-name dispersion high.

In investment grade, UBS favors medium maturities from A/BBB rated names in defensive sectors (utilities, telecoms, energy), plus select industrials and national champion banks. It also likes covered bonds and infrastructure-backed credits as sovereign alternatives.

In high yield, UBS favors higher-quality issuers with resilient business models, solid free cash flow and manageable refinancing. It sees value in selected hybrids from quality financial and non-financial issuers as an alternative to traditional high yield.

UBS avoids M&A candidates, expensive consumer discretionary names, EUR real estate and some regional specialised lenders in IG, and autos, chemicals and other structurally challenged credits in high yield.
Euro IG OAS is 107bp, up 18bp since the last NVT and 29bp YTD. Euro HY OAS is 362bp, up 62bp since the last NVT and 92bp YTD. CCC & lower Euro HY is at 1792bp, up 352bp since the last NVT.

US credit spreads moved less than euro spreads. US IG OAS is 88bp (+4bp since the last NVT, +9bp YTD) and US HY OAS is 318bp (+6bp since the last NVT, +37bp YTD). BB US HY OAS tightened 7bp to 187bp. CCC & lower US HY widened 142bp to 1321bp.
UBS describes corporate spreads as back to peak Iran war levels.

Sovereign debt affordability is strained by higher yields. The US, Japan, France and Belgium are likely to see the largest rise in debt servicing costs, worst when much debt matures soon and new debt costs far more than existing debt.

Where growth cannot offset higher yields, UBS expects governments to use a mix of fiscal adjustment and financial repression to lower real yields. The US and Japan have more scope for yield-containing measures. European countries may need fiscal reforms. Measures to cut real yields should help bonds but can hurt the currency.
UBS expects Germany to keep its AAA ratings from Moody's, S&P and Fitch and sees its debt burden as highly manageable. Bunds are a scarce, liquid benchmark asset with a structural safe-haven role.

UBS keeps a Deteriorating issuer credit outlook on France and expects the first agency to cut France to the mid-A level by 2027. Current ratings are Moody's Aa3 negative, S&P A+ stable, Fitch A+ stable. France should stay in the A category through 2030.

French bonds trade wider than BBB-rated Italian bonds across the curve, which UBS reads as fiscal concerns already priced in. Heavy supply and reduced foreign buying make valuations sensitive. UBS prefers the short to mid part of the sovereign and agency curves and sees pre-election spread spikes as possible entry points.

Recent French spread moves are small against history if France is viewed as trading like a credit, as Italy and Spain do. French all-in yields have reached 5%, against a 7.5% peak for Spain in 2012 and 3.6% for Italy in 2018.

trade_ideas.rationale: High carry yields make positive 12-month total returns very likely.
trade_ideas.risk: Uncertainty around growth, inflation, geopolitics and trade policy, plus issuer-specific risks and M&A.

trade_ideas.rationale: Rating downgrades are already priced in, and French bonds trade wider than BBB-rated Italian ones across the curve.
trade_ideas.risk: Heavy supply and reduced foreign buying make valuations sensitive.

risk_factors: Delayed decline in inflation from re-accelerating energy end-product prices and possible El Niño-related food price inflation.
Stronger-than-expected US and European growth could keep central banks restrictive.
Low margin for error in tight credit markets.
Single-name dispersion from M&A activity, bond supply and issuer-specific risks.
Rising debt servicing costs in the US, Japan, France and Belgium.
Financial repression measures that lower real yields may weaken currencies.
French fiscal consolidation is unlikely, with a possible rating downgrade by 2027, heavy supply and reduced foreign demand.
